set.n: Louis Hoffman's buried kettle ('$30,000', sworn at $35), Nordman's hill, 2 mi S of New London
set.st: Farmer Louis Hoffman dug up a buried cache on Nordman's hill; the first reports put it at about $30,000 and said it lay under a tree in his orchard; origin a mystery. Pin is approximate, not the spot itself. The 1889 Waupaca County plat shows "C. Nordman 160" on the SE¼ of sec. 24 T22N R14E (Mukwa), about 2 miles south-southeast of New London: that is Nordman's hill. The pin is the centre of that quarter (BLM section lines). The wallet was dug up under an orchard tree on Nordman's Hill, 2 miles south of New London, some weeks before 29 Jan 1908. It is thought to have been buried by a farmhand who called himself "Harry Palmer of Chicago". He vanished, was arrested in Chicago for robbery and killed himself in jail. No owner of the money was ever found. 1938 aerial: no farmstead in the quarter by 1938; the old orchard and the hill are in the SW part of SE¼ sec. 24 T22N R14E, where the pin now sits (it was formerly in sec. 19 of the next range). Outcome: the May 1908 wire says he struck an iron kettle of gold, silver and notes while digging stumps in a pasture, and Mrs Catherine Schmall, widow of a former owner, Henry Schmall, sued for it under the discovery statutes. On 8 May 1908 Hoffman testified in county court at Appleton that the find was worth only $35, and the case ended. The January accounts say orchard tree, the May wire says pasture stumps; same farm and same find.
set.t: Found and settled in court: the sworn value was $35. Record only. Access: private.

src: Wisconsin State Journal, 2 May 1908, p. 1 (newspapers.com 397137380) and Green Bay Press-Gazette, 2 May 1908, p. 1 (186429970): one wire, kettle and Schmall suit
Stoughton Weekly Courier-Hub, 15 May 1908, p. 2 (newspapers.com 1081066853): Appleton 8 May, Hoffman swears the find was worth $35

set.tovw: Hidden shortly before death, family search unsuccessful 1906; nothing later
